summary: Defines a new object for RSVP-TE messages that carries extra attribute flags for MPLS label switched paths, since the eight-bit Flags field of the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object was nearly used up. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4420 and updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5420 adds a flexible way for RSVP-TE messages to carry extra properties of an MPLS path. It also lets routers report which properties they applied, while distinguishing information that some routers may pass along from requirements every transit router must understand.

subtitle: How RSVP-TE carries extensible attributes for MPLS paths and records which routers apply them.

tldr.problem: The RSVP-TE SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object has an eight-bit Flags field, and only three bits remained available as proposals sought more options. That leaves little room for future LSP attributes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5420 defines two RSVP objects built from type-length-value fields: one that can pass through routers that do not understand it, and one that every transit router must inspect. A Record Route subobject can report attributes hop by hop.
tldr.outcome: It provides an extensible way to signal and record LSP attributes. RFC 5420 obsoletes RFC 4420 and is updated by RFC 6510.

today: RFC 5420 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4420, updates RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, and has been updated by RFC 6510.

sections.title: Why RSVP-TE Needs More Attribute Space
sections.content:
Traffic-engineered Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) paths, called Label Switched Paths (LSPs), can be established with RSVP-TE Path messages. These messages already carry a SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object with an eight-bit Flags field.

Three bits were assigned in RFC 3209 and two in RFC 4090, leaving three unassigned. Other proposals also needed bits, so RFC 5420 adds new objects made from type-length-value (TLV) fields. They carry more flag bits and can carry other attribute parameters. The same mechanisms apply to Generalized MPLS packet-switch-capable and non-packet-switch-capable LSPs.

The RFC keeps the older SESSION_ATTRIBUTE options in place. It distinguishes attributes that only selected routers need to inspect from attributes that all transit routers must handle.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing RSVP-TE options field had only a few unused bits. This RFC defines separate message objects so later specifications can add attributes without changing that crowded field.

sections.title: Attribute TLVs and Flag Bits
sections.content:
Each attribute object contains one or more TLVs: a Type, a Length and a Value. Type identifies the kind of information. Length counts the full TLV, including its Type and Length fields, but not any padding. The TLV is padded with up to three zero octets to align it to four octets. TLVs have no required order.

RFC 5420 defines TLV Type 1, the Attribute Flags TLV. Its value contains groups of 32 flag bits, numbered from the most significant bit with bit zero. Unassigned bits must be sent as zero. Any bit absent from the TLV, or an absent TLV, is treated as zero. This RFC assigns no individual attribute bits.

A later specification defining a bit must say whether the bit is used in the optional attributes object, the required attributes object, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLV labels a piece of data and gives its length. In the flag TLV, a missing or unset bit means the attribute is not requested.

sections.title: Attributes That Routers May Pass Along
sections.content:
The LSP_ATTRIBUTES object carries attributes that do not require every transit Label Switching Router (LSR) to act. An LSR that does not recognize the object passes it on unchanged, allowing it to cross routers that do not support the extension. Its RSVP class number is 197 and its C-Type is 1.

A router that recognizes the object but not one of its TLVs must pass that TLV unchanged. The same rule applies to an unrecognized set bit in the Attribute Flags TLV. The specification defining a recognized but unsupported attribute says what the router must do.

The object can also appear in a Resv message to report operational state for the whole LSP. A router may set or clear a bit as the attribute definition directs. This report does not give per-router state; the Record Route subobject handles that.
sections.plainLanguage: This object can carry an attribute past routers that do not understand it. Routers that do understand it follow the rules written for that particular attribute.

sections.title: Attributes Every Transit Router Must Inspect
sections.content:
The LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object carries attributes that every transit LSR must examine. A router must not forward the object without acting on its contents. Its RSVP class number is 67 and its C-Type is 1.

A router that does not recognize this object rejects the Path message with an Unknown Object Class error. A router that recognizes the object but not a TLV rejects the message with Unknown Attributes TLV. An unrecognized flag bit causes an Unknown Attributes Bit error. A later specification defines the behavior for a recognized attribute the router cannot support.

This object is used on Path messages, not Resv messages. Status can instead be reported in an LSP_ATTRIBUTES object on Resv or in a per-hop Record Route subobject.
sections.plainLanguage: This object marks an attribute as something every transit router must understand. A router that cannot recognize it rejects the path instead of silently passing it along.

sections.title: Inheritance and Per-Hop Recording
sections.content:
At a forwarding-adjacency LSP boundary, local policy may allow the new LSP to inherit some attributes from the LSP that caused it to be set up. By default, no incoming attributes are inherited. Each specification that defines an attribute bit must say whether it can be inherited.

The Record Route object can include an Attributes subobject to record information for a particular hop. Its flag numbers correspond to those in the Attribute Flags TLV. A router pushes this subobject just before its address or interface identifier, and must not push it without also recording one of those identifiers.

A router may set a bit to report compliance with a requested attribute or clear it to report non-compliance, as that attribute's definition requires. Unset bits, bits beyond a short subobject, and bits for a hop without the subobject are treated as zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can record attribute results beside their own addresses in the route record. Missing bits count as zero, and attributes are not inherited by default when a new forwarding-adjacency path is created.

sections.title: Where the Objects Appear in RSVP Messages
sections.content:
A Path message may carry either or both attribute objects. The recommended position is after SESSION_ATTRIBUTE, or after LABEL_REQUEST if there is no session attribute. When both are present, the required-attributes object is recommended first. Routers must accept them in any position and forward subsequent duplicate instances unchanged while ignoring them.

A Resv message may carry LSP_ATTRIBUTES in the flow descriptor associated with the preceding FILTER_SPEC. Only one such object is meaningful for that filter specification; later instances should be ignored and must be forwarded unchanged.

The order recommendations do not change the requirement that implementations accept the objects in any meaningful order.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC recommends where to place these objects, but routers must handle them wherever they appear in a message. Duplicate objects are passed onward without changing them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says these objects and the Record Route subobject introduce no new direct security issues. It refers readers to the security considerations in RFC 2205, RFC 3209 and RFC 3473.

Attribute requests can reveal LSP preferences to someone who can read signaling messages. Per-hop records can reveal LSP state and the capabilities of individual routers. The RFC says encryption of signaling messages can address disclosure, while noting a tension between informing the path head end and hiding transit routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Attribute messages and route records may reveal information about a path and its routers. The RFC points to the existing RSVP security guidance and identifies encryption as a way to protect signaling contents.
